question: In a standard holding pattern, in which direction are the turns flown?

options.text: To the right (clockwise)
To the left (counter-clockwise)
Alternating left and right on successive orbits
Whichever direction the wind is blowing from

explanation: A standard hold uses right-hand turns throughout; a non-standard hold is one published or issued with left-hand turns instead.

question: What is the standard outbound leg time for a holding pattern flown below 14,000 ft?

options.text: 30 seconds
1 minute
1.5 minutes
2 minutes

explanation: Below 14,000 ft the standard outbound leg is timed at 1 minute; above 14,000 ft it is extended to 1.5 minutes to account for higher true airspeed.

question: Which holding entry is used when the aircraft approaches the fix from roughly within the "direct" sector relative to the inbound holding course?

options.text: Parallel entry
Teardrop (offset) entry
Direct entry
Racetrack entry

explanation: A direct entry is flown by crossing the fix and turning directly onto the outbound leg, used when the aircraft's approach track falls within the direct-entry sector.

question: What shape does a standard holding pattern trace over the ground in still air?

options.text: A perfect circle
A racetrack shape, formed by two straight legs joined by two 180-degree turns
A figure-eight
A square with four 90-degree turns

explanation: The classic holding pattern is a racetrack: an inbound leg to the fix, a 180-degree turn, an outbound leg, and another 180-degree turn back onto the inbound leg.

question: Why does a pilot apply wind correction while flying a holding pattern?

options.text: Wind correction is never necessary once established in a hold
To keep the aircraft's ground track close to the charted holding pattern despite drift, adjusting heading on each leg and turn
Only to increase groundspeed on the outbound leg
Only to correct for magnetic variation between fixes

explanation: Without wind correction the pattern would drift downwind of the fix; pilots adjust heading on each leg (and often the timing) to keep the pattern over the protected airspace it was designed for.

question: In a "parallel" holding pattern entry, what does the aircraft do immediately after crossing the fix?

options.text: Turns directly onto the inbound holding course
Flies outbound parallel to the inbound holding course, on the non-holding side, before turning back to intercept and re-cross the fix
Flies a track 90 degrees offset from the holding course, away from the pattern
Flies the outbound leg on the holding side, opposite to the direct entry

explanation: A parallel entry tracks outbound parallel to the inbound course on the non-holding side, then turns to intercept the inbound course and re-cross the fix before joining the pattern normally.

question: Before entering a holding pattern that was not already part of the published/cleared route, what must a pilot normally have?

options.text: Nothing further — a hold may always be entered without clearance
An ATC clearance to hold, which may include an expect-further-clearance time
A descent clearance to the minimum sector altitude first
Cancellation of the IFR flight plan

explanation: Holding is an ATC-directed procedure; a pilot needs a clearance to hold (with details such as the holding fix, direction, leg length and an expect-further-clearance time) unless already published as part of the cleared route.

question: If the outbound leg of a hold is flown with a tailwind (having had a headwind inbound), how should the outbound leg timing generally be adjusted?

options.text: No adjustment is needed
Shorten the outbound leg time, so the inbound leg comes as close as possible to the standard time
Lengthen the outbound leg regardless of wind
Change holding altitude instead of adjusting timing

explanation: Because the inbound leg's time is what matters for the pattern to stay within protected airspace, pilots shorten the outbound leg when it has a tailwind, so the return leg — now flown into a headwind — still times close to the standard duration.
